title: Sandworm_Backdoor_Investigation_685
description: You are an incident responder tasked with investigating a potential compromise involving the Sandworm malware family, specifically the Exaramel backdoor. This backdoor is known to ensure persistence via a scheduled task (Cron) and communicates with its command and control (C2) servers via HTTPS. Your mission is to identify, investigate, and mitigate the threat.
outcomes: Identify and investigate unauthorized or suspicious services running on a host.
Determine how the suspicious service is automatically started after reboot.
Locate the executable or file associated with the suspicious activity.

levels.title: Introduction
levels.content: You are an incident responder tasked with investigating a potential compromise involving the Sandworm malware family, specifically the Exaramel backdoor. This backdoor is known to ensure persistence via a scheduled task (Cron) and communicates with its command and control (C2) servers via HTTPS. Your mission is to identify, investigate, and mitigate the threat.

levels.title: Get Access
levels.cloud_content: Access the target host via SSH using the username 'user' and password 'password'. Enter 'start' to begin.
levels.local_content: Access the target host via SSH using the username 'user' and password 'password'. Enter 'start' to begin.

levels.title: Suspicious Service Discovery
levels.content: While monitoring the network, you noticed unusual outbound HTTPS traffic from the target host. Investigate the target host to identify any unauthorized or suspicious services running that could be responsible for this traffic.
levels.solution: To identify the suspicious service, you can use the command `systemctl list-units --type=service` to list all running services. Look for any services that seem out of place or unfamiliar. The suspicious service in this case is `bkd.service`.

hints.title: First hint title
hints.content: Check the running services and look for any that seem out of place or unfamiliar.

hints.title: Second hint title
hints.content: Use the command `systemctl list-units --type=service` to list all running services.

hints.title: Third hint title
hints.content: The suspicious service is likely to have an unusual name or be located in an unexpected directory.

levels.title: Persistence Discovery
levels.content: Now that you have identified the suspicious service, determine how it is automatically started after a system reboot. This will help you understand the persistence mechanism used by the malware.
levels.solution: To determine the persistence mechanism, you can use the command `systemctl list-timers` to list all systemd timers. Look for any timers that are associated with the suspicious service. The persistence mechanism in this case is `lab-checkin.timer`.

hints.title: First hint title
hints.content: Investigate systemd services and timers to find how the service is scheduled to run.

hints.title: Second hint title
hints.content: Use the command `systemctl list-timers` to list all systemd timers.

hints.title: Third hint title
hints.content: The timer associated with the suspicious service is likely to have a name that includes 'checkin' or 'update'.

levels.title: Suspicious File Discovery
levels.content: Locate the executable or file associated with the suspicious service you identified earlier. This will help you gather more information about the malware and its behavior.
levels.solution: To locate the executable or file associated with the suspicious service, you can use the command `systemctl cat bkd.service` to view the service configuration file. Look for the executable path in the configuration file. The file associated with the suspicious service in this case is `/usr/local/bin/lab-checkin.sh`.

hints.title: First hint title
hints.content: Check the service configuration files and look for the executable path.

hints.title: Second hint title
hints.content: Use the command `systemctl cat bkd.service` to view the service configuration file.

hints.title: Third hint title
hints.content: The executable path is likely to be in a directory such as /usr/local/bin or /opt.
